utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Now, we have submissions, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Your Honour, yesterday I asked your leave to address you on two points. The first point is the medical report, or rather, the addendum to the medical report, as ordered by Your Honours on the 4th of February this year. Yesterday we submitted the annex to the medical report, and in the view of the Defence all the issues that were raised have been addressed in this report, according to Your Honours' decision. I will not, of course, go into the content of this report because I do not feel competent to make any judgements about it. Of course this is up to you, Your Honours, and others whose job it will be to judge the content of that report. However, in our view the report establishes the necessary link which was perhaps not sufficiently evident in the original report, that is, the link between the diagnosis, the symptoms, and the influence of these on the key aspects of the ability of the accused to stand trial, that is, to follow the proceedings, to understand the proceedings, to give instructions to his counsel, to possibly testify before the Bench, and to understand all the consequences of what is happening before this Tribunal. In our view, this link is now completely clear and the material is now complete and that it forms a sufficient basis for a decision. We will not burden you any further. We hold that the report is now complete. We also abide by what we said previously on this issue, and that is the readiness and openness of our side and our client to have the content of this report verified. As Your Honours ordered last Wednesday, we submitted the written consent of our client and our written consent to allow access to our learned friends to all the documents now in the Detention Unit. Last Thursday we delivered to them, or rather, we delivered to the Detention Unit our written consent. I would also like to mention that most of the documents, in addition to the clinical analysis and the tests carried out by the expert, all the other documents that Mr. Strugar brought with him on the 12th of December are now in the Detention Unit. They have been handed over to the medical service of the Detention Unit. Unfortunately, I have to say that my learned friends from the Prosecution took steps to gain access to these documents only yesterday, so that yesterday there was very lively activity. In order to implement all this, there is a certain delay, but we hope that my learned friends will have all these documents in their possession today, or at the latest on Monday. We wish to reiterate that as soon as Your Honours so ordered, we did submit our written consent and our client's written consent. And if my learned friends still feel that there is need for additional information in addition to the report of Mrs. Tusevski, we hope that this matter will then proceed further, that all the necessary tests will be carried out. And, Your Honours, I'm willing to answer any questions you may have or any question my learned friend, Ms. Somers, may have. Thank you, Your Honour. By your leave, Your Honour, I will address the second point I wish to raise when we have concluded discussing the first topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. The Chamber takes it from all you have said that the two reports now that you have obtained from Dr. Lecic, together with the earlier medical reports and papers that have been brought across with your client provide the foundation for the Defence's submission that the Chamber should terminate the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the situation is as follows: The report of Dr. Lecic of the 2nd of February and the additional report that was submitted to you yesterday is the basis for this. Why? Because none of the previous medical reports dealt specifically with the ability of the accused to stand trial. The doctors who examined him previously treated various aspects of his ailments, but there was no synthesis made of this and no assessment by a court expert. This is the only synthetic evaluation covering all the aspects of the psychological and somatic status of the accused. This is, therefore, the basis. Because none of the previous documents was all-encompassing. None of them contained an overall analysis. They contained the case history, which was then amplified by the clinical evaluation of the doctor and the battery of tests that were carried out in order to assess the psychological status of the accused. We submit, therefore, that the basis for our motion is the report and the addendum to the report, while all the other documents comprise the case history, the medical history, which of course goes to support the final report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you very much. Addressing firstly the addendum. The Prosecution wishes to inform the Chamber that upon the initial arising of this question, it made its initial inquiries of various professionals as to the testing. The decision on documents is based on the fact that what the Prosecution needs first and foremost is films. We need the actual MRI, virtually every professional we have spoken to has insisted on a current MRI, not a two-year-old MRI from Podgorica, Montenegro. The inherent reliability of the report based on a two-year-old MRI is obvious. Accordingly one of the first things we will have to seek from the Chamber is an order that an MRI be performed by a highly professional institution under -- in the Netherlands under the most efficient laboratory conditions available. And we will make the appropriate requests in writing as we progress. But I do want to emphasise that that is a critical first starting point. And it is my understand that the films are not here from Montenegro, that we have nothing but reports. Perhaps counsel can inform us at a later time, but that is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: From what you say whether the earlier MRI results were available or not, those you have consulted would want a new test?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. The importance of having the MRIs is for comparative bases, perhaps no different than traditional testing that is done in any comparative study and also, of course, to ensure that the subject is the subject. Secondly, I note that the addendum appears more to be an apology, as it were, in defence of comments made on the record as -- not an apology in an excuse me apology, but a defensive apology of the psychiatrist as opposed to addressing, really, how in whatever consultations were made, the criteria that the Prosecution set forth preliminarily were met. There is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Somers, can I say from the Chamber's point of view the two reports that are now before us of Dr. Lecic form the basis of the application for the Defence. As the Chamber has indicated, we regard the first report on its own as sufficient to validly raise the issue of the competence of the accused to stand trial. The further report is in support of that, so that I don't think it's really helpful today to put submissions as to the merit and quality of those reports. We're really concerned with what is the Prosecution's position now and what it needs to do and wishes to do about any examination before the Chamber considers how to determine this application.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do understand that. The Prosecution will undertake its own expert evaluation. It is in the process of doing so. We are consulting with preeminent neuropsychiatrists from both the United Kingdom and the United States at this point and we are -- that has not been the parameters of the search. We are looking really for the top people in the field. We also understand that timing, because good people will not be available on a day's notice, that timing is going to be an issue, and we are -- once the preliminary issues of accepting the terms of employment with the United Nations -- I -- have been dealt with -- we are providing the relevant information as we get it. We will seek the current MRI. We will have a -- we will seek to have a neuroradiologist interpret the MRI. We will seek to have a neuropsychologist if possible, administer the appropriate cognisant tests which are not discussed in the reports on which the Defence is placing its case and a neuropsychiatrist to review the findings and to do a clinical analysis, in other words to meet with the accused and to perform the testing. That is the plan, and this has been consistent with the conversations with the professionals with whom we have dealt, that this is the best way to go. We -- for purposes of proceeding further, if the Chamber would want us to direct our submissions now to the motion that was filed, and I'll wait for guidance on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. What we need to know clearly and I think we understand it from what you've said already, that you do propose to seek to have examined the accused with a view to gaining your own opinions on the competence of the accused to stand trial. And I think that's what needs to be addressed today and that we need it from you an indication of the timetable which you see. Because it is of grave concern to the Chamber that this matter needs to be dealt with as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is also obviously for us the same concern, Your Honour. I appreciate that. The timing would be -- at least to get the preliminaries within the next two weeks, based on the availability of the particular doctors with whom we are speaking. We would need a Court order, a Chamber order, for an MRI to be done directed to Registry. In order to have the appropriate prescription, as it were, for the MRI, MRI of, we would ask for enough time to have the examining or the lead doctor give us that so we can put it in an appropriate order, lest there be any misunderstanding and the tests are tests that require both timing to -- or time to have ordered and have expense involved. So that would be the first request. And we will undertake to try to have some answer I would say within about seven to ten days. One person with whom we're very interested in working is away. And if this person does undertake the assignment, then we would need to allow sufficient time for his return to his home base. Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's not terribly clear to me about what you are saying about the time that you need to be in a position to have the reports you want to put before the Chamber in answer to the reports of Dr. Lecic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For the final reports, Your Honour, I would not envision earlier than after an MRI, after an MRI has been done and interpreted. I would imagine we're probably looking at three to four weeks because of the testing and the ability in the system to actually have a filed, assessed report. Now, if we have to change the area of search based on a timetable that is different here - and we appreciate that the trial is not a long trial - but the timing also of the motion puts us all in a difficult position. Had it been raised at a different time, we might have been able to have jumped it more early. But I don't want to put something before the Court that I could not deliver. If the Chamber instructs that we narrow the search and try to move with a more readily available -- I mean, the people we are trying to get are very, very good people. This is my honest assessment. I would not foresee it earlier than perhaps three weeks. We have to get the person in, we have to get the examination done, and we have to have the MRI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, thank you for waiting. You have been on your feet. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I must comment on what my learned friend has said. The plan that my learned friend envisages of three to four weeks and then four to five weeks, this in fact means that this trial will be over for the most part and that we at present have only one report which indicates that the accused is not competent and unable to follow the trial. The circumstances demand, Your Honours, that this be dealt with extremely expeditiously. Needless to say, we are now in a highly civilised country, and I am sure that any urgent medical examination can be done very, very soon. This is the experience of all of us here at this Tribunal. Therefore, I cannot believe that it would take four weeks to have something done that can be done tomorrow morning. I ask for your understanding, Your Honours. An MRI can also be done in the Bronovo Hospital, which is 2 kilometres away from this institution. It's not necessary for an expert to come in from the U.S.A. I'm sure that a Dutch expert in the Westeinde Hospital or in the Bronovo Hospital is just as highly qualified as somebody who might come in from the U.S.A. We don't have to wait for somebody to travel across the ocean when it could be done by somebody in our neighbourhood. If we look at this way, Your Honours, then our request gains in strength. Otherwise, if it is really necessary to have experts come in from the U.S.A, I ask that the proceedings be interrupted and that there be a delay until this is done. We believe that it is not necessary to wait so long, and we ask for your intervention. Secondly, Your Honours, of course the Defence does not object to an MRI of the accused's head. On the contrary, we fully support this proposal. This is something that was done in Podgorica. The image is in the Detention Unit. This is something that is exact and not subject to various interpretations, but we do not challenge the right of the Prosecution to have this done. We, as laymen, have sought information on the nature of this illness, and this is an irreversible process. It's a process of multiple strokes in the brain, and it is something that can only get worse, that cannot get better. But of course this will be subject to the expert assessment of the Prosecution's expert. What I have not heard in my learned friend's submissions is the following: The MRI is only one aspect of the three psychiatric diagnosis in this report. This is something that has to do with vascular dementia. However, there are two other diagnoses and there is the overall synthesis. The issue of Depression and the issue of PTSD. Depression and PTSD are not something that can be diagnosed through an MRI; this is something that has to be diagnosed by a psychiatrist. We fully support this first submission that has to do with vascular dementia. But if the Prosecutor doubts the entire report she should also work very fast on finding a psychiatrist to evaluate the other two diagnoses and the overall diagnosis. I refer to the jurisprudence prudence of this Tribunal. In almost every case where a psychiatric evaluation was done, a psychiatric evaluation that has to do with the psychological status irrespective of the MRI or the CT or any other test. In all the cases I am familiar with are at least in the vast majority of cases, this was done by somebody who speaks the language of the accused. To do a psychological evaluation, a psychiatric evaluation, through an interpreter, this is something where a lot can get lost. Only direct contact can enable the psychiatrist to carry out an assessment. What I am trying to say is that this psychiatrist should be somebody from Belgrade or Podgorica. Your Honours, you know that people from many other countries in the western Balkans speak similar languages, so the expert can also be from Sarajevo or from Zagreb or any other part of the former Yugoslavia where languages are spoken that the accused understands. The expert can also be from the U.S. if he understands the language of the accused. But to carry out a psychiatric evaluation through an interpreter would mean losing a vast amount of necessary information. So please bear this in mind, Your Honours. This has been the practice in the vast majority of the cases known to this Defence team before this Tribunal. Therefore, Your Honours, I ask you -- well, first of all, I fully support what Ms. Somers has said about the MRI of the brain, and I ask that this be done as soon as possible. And also I would ask Your Honours to establish a very strict and limited timetable, one measured in days not in months, Your Honour. What my learned friend is suggesting would take months, and months would take us to an appeal, possibly. Therefore, I ask Your Honours to act promptly in this case. Should this not be possible, I ask that the proceedings be interrupted until my learned friend can get all the information she needs. I don't think this is in the interest of any of us, however. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. There's some very valid observations there. But I understand from what you said earlier, Ms. Somers, that you not only are contemplating the need, as a first step, for an MRI examination and its interpretation by a neuroradiologist. And you were also looking at a neuropsychologist and a neuropsychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct. We're looking at -- it's clearly a multidisciplinary endeavour. And Thank you for letting me continue my submissions. I wasn't contemplating the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought you had finished. I do beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, it's okay. I appreciate -- I wanted to make sure that a couple of points were made. First of all, we were -- we did not -- I don't see that five weeks was part of our submission. We are trying to be very realistic. This is, really, the first -- this would become the first fitness hearing probably in -- I may not speak for all Tribunals, but certainly in this Tribunal, and we are mindful of the importance of making sure that it is done in the most appropriate manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And from the Chamber's point of view, relevant and significant in that is time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, we understand that. And the issue of -- I believe Defence counsel has not understood that we are not suggesting that an MRI specialist come over from any other place. But the Dutch system is fine and Bronovo hospital would be a very appropriate place to have it done. It is certainly a superb institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we cut to the core then. The Chamber would look to receive from you today, if it were feasible, the order that you would propose for the MRI. There is no objection to such a test as long as it is framed with the medical detail that we would need our assistance on. You can expect that the Chamber would grant that order. And in view of all that you've said and the need for urgency in the case and what Mr. Petrovic has said, we would take the view that it ought to be feasible to -- for the Prosecution to be in a position to have its report before the Chamber in three weeks from now. And that is what we would see as the timetable. It's not the months that Mr. Petrovic feared, nor is it quite the days that I think he had hoped for, but it is in view of all that has to be done and what you have put, we think an adequate time. Now, we leave it entirely to your judgement who and how you achieve the result. And the fact is relevant and that will include the need to be in a position to put the necessary report or reports before us within three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I inquire on one point. Mr. Petrovic presupposed that the MRI was only of the brain. In fact, the report discusses a number of other organic issues and I suspect it will not be limited just to one particular area and that a full and cooperative examination by the accused will be, I'm sure, sought by the examining physicians. And we are also -- when we told the Chamber what we had hoped to be able to line up, this is the hope. If the time frame changes any aspect of the multidisciplinary team, then of course we will proceed as time and resources permit, still with the idea of giving the Chamber the most helpful possible report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I certainly understand from Mr. Petrovic that the relevance of the other physical conditions is seen to be a relevant and significant aspect. And a full examination by MRI of any of those possible symptoms would seem to be sensible. Would that not be the case Mr. Petrovic? You're getting instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, I was not in a position to hear exactly what you just told me. I apologise on behalf of my colleagues and my client. I again must apologise to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise for this inconvenience that we have just caused the Chamber. We were trying to consult our client in this matter. His hearing seems to be a further problem. What Mr. Rodic has just found out from our client is that the MRI scan of the lower half of the body was done just before our client arrived here. So it is not certain that -- at any rate, the doctors will see. Once he arrived in the Detention Unit, the scan was done. So the lower half of his body was done -- was scanned here. It has been available since the 12th of December, so there's no need to go through that again. As for the other thing that my colleague has talked about, this is true, this was done two years ago, and there is no problem for that to be done again. But I would ask again for the Chamber to take into consideration the fact that part of this team at least, which needs -- must be an interdisciplinary team must be from the former Yugoslavia, those who will conduct the clinical examination of the accused must be someone who shares the same language, because the very validity of their report rests on that. It is not possible to have this done through an interpreter; that's what experience teaches us. This may as well be someone from Zagreb or, perhaps even to push it to an extreme, somebody from Dubrovnik. The important thing is that the expert speaks the language of the accused. This is our submission, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will look into the availability of any recent films on the accused. And I would like simply to make a record comment that those of us from multicultural jurisdictions who have worked through interpretation for a long time find that the proposition that through -- working through translation is an inefficient tool; that simply is not the case. And whether we select to have someone who is from the former Yugoslavia or someone who simply is a translator who can work well with a skilled professional will be within the -- certainly within the discretion of the Prosecution. And that we would -- our experience in interviewing very eminent professionals is that because they come from jurisdictions where not everyone is speaking the same language, they have to work quite a bit through interpretation, which is not a new phenomenon. And accordingly we will certainly make sure that it is clear that language has to be very much factored in. But this is not something that I is within the sound province of the Defence to settle. Thank you very much. And we will report back. If there is any issue next week, we will submit. We can preliminarily request the prescription for a description of the MRI so we can get it to the Chamber. If the professional is not able to get it because of a time change today, is Monday satisfactory for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can't imagine that you will get any full MRI done over the weekend if it's not an emergency. So Monday will meet that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Something further, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies for taking up too much time this morning. In view of what my learned friend and colleague has just said, she knows full well, and so do I, in many cases that she, too, was part of and that I was part of. How the issue of psychiatric expert opinion was dealt with, in terms of the language being spoken. We can go back into private session to enumerate the cases in which psychiatrists from the same language area as the accused conducted such examinations. This has been the case in most instances. My learned friend has been part of these cases and so has the Defence team. There is no need to point out who the Prosecution enlisted for this job or the Trial Chamber or the representative Defence teams. One of these -- one of the members of these teams invariably was someone who understands and shares the language of the accused. If you have an interpreter, you can see for yourselves, Your Honours, how many problems we encounter in our daily work here in terms of interpretation. We fully respect the degree of difficulty involved in their work, but there are problems on a daily basis. You are perfectly able to imagine how difficult it must be when we are talking about a psychiatric evaluation of someone who has a mental condition. Nuances of translation become highly important. It is very important to see all the nuances of meaning once the report is drawn up. This is of the utmost importance. And this has been the established practice in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Obviously, experts all over the world are welcome to contribute their expertise to this institution. However, in this specific case I don't think we can replace experts from the former Yugoslavia when we talk about psychiatric evaluations of the accused. This is specific to the case in hand, and I believe this should be taken into account by the Chamber. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are of the view that given the difficulties that have faced with finding people with appropriate qualification and experience in the limited time that we feel this issue must be dealt with, that it would be wrong to give any direction that people of a particular language skill should be chosen. But we are very sympathetic to the common sense of what has been put to us by Mr. Petrovic, and we would indicate that it is likely to be a factor which we will take into account. Should there be a difference of opinion emerge between the psychiatrists and others consulted by the Prosecution and the reports we already have from Dr. Lecic, we will see it as relevant and will take into account, should the examination and assessment by a psychiatrist be -- and a psychologist be one that is undertaken through an interpreter rather than by a medical expert who shares the language and culture of the accused. Now, we have there, Ms. Somers, gone out of our way, perhaps, not to tie your hands too much, but I am sure you will take into account the value for this type of examination and assessment of choosing people who do not have to work through an interpreter. The Chamber will therefore leave the matter on this basis. Either today or Monday, we will receive from the Prosecution the order which they seek for an MRI examination of the brain at least. Whether there is need for it to be of the body will depend upon inquiries, I am sure that will be made, whether there is, as has been indicated, a current MRI scan available of the other relevant parts of the body of the accused. And we will look for the report or reports within three weeks of the MRI scan being made. Now, Mr. Petrovic, the second matter you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies for taking up so much of our time this morning, but we believe that these were important issues to be raised and that ultimately this will contribute to expedite proceedings. The other thing I wanted to bring up on behalf of Mr. Strugar's defence, if the Chamber could possibly take into account the following: To have a brief pause in these proceedings. Why is it that we are requesting this? I will try to be brief. First of all, I wish to say that I have brought this up before with my learned friends from the OTP, and I wish to point out - they will no doubt correct me if I'm wrong - that they have shown a great deal of understanding for problems that we have presented. They will not take up any particular position on this; they will leave it to the Chamber, to the Chamber's discretion, to decide. The reasons are as follows: I would like to, please, briefly go into private session for the first reason I am about to bring up. I would not like it to be made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The reason for that, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the reason is personal and it pertains to a request in relation to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're asking me and the Chamber to be just a little -- resting a little lightly on the Rules which stipulate particular reasons why we should go into private. If you will be quick, we will go into private.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to oblige. You won't believe how brief I can be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I look forward to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope, Your Honours, that I have complied with your instructions in terms of brevity. This was the first thing I wish to raise. There is another reason, too, which I would like to speak about now. There are two further reasons that the Defence team wishes to address. As you know, Your Honours, we have been here on the ground for over a month now. We have people back home conducting investigations on our behalf. However, since more than a month we have been in touch by telephone with these people working for us; however, some things just cannot be discussed on the phone and must be dealt with directly. It's about gathering evidence, and some issues are simply too sensitive to be dealt with, like this, over the phone. There is a need to get in direct contact with these people, at least for a brief period of time. Some of the instructions can be forwarded over the telephone, but some can't. As we have been informed that there are a number of witnesses that these people have contacted and that may be potentially important witnesses for us and for our case; however, even with full respect for the work of our people on the ground, these witnesses are adamant that they want to speak to one of the people directly involved in the trial, meaning myself or my colleague, Mr. Rodic. The third reason relates to the expert witness reports that we -- that have finally been disclosed to us in English and B/C/S last Wednesday, if I'm not mistaken. Now we get to the issue of our own experts who have to provide their own opinion. We are talking to our experts on the phone, however the sheer scope of the problem is such that part of it can be dealt with over the phone, but some of it needs to be gone through in the physical presence of these people who provide us with their expertise. Your Honours, this is only possible if we are actually physically in their presence and in direct touch with them. We are well aware that time is a major concern for this Trial Chamber, but we have brought up these three different groups of reasons. And I believe it would be in the interests of justice for you to perhaps allow us to pause in the first week of March. I spoke to Ms. Somers about this, and as far as I understand there has not been any prearrangement that has been for the witnesses in that particular week; therefore, we would not be disrupting the -- an already existing schedule. By your leave, even Ms. Somers would be able to comply with that schedule, should the Trial Chamber allow to have a week's interruption in the proceedings in the first week of March. This is our request. Thank you very much, Your Honours, and we believe that we will have your understanding in these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, two issues. Firstly, you feel a week at about that time would accommodate both the anxiety of the accused, to be able to spend some time with his wife. And secondly, the needs of the Defence to pursue certain detailed preparation of your case, interviewing witnesses and consulting experts. A week will deal with all of these issues; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, that's what I'm saying. All these things could be done in the course of that week. We will make sure to make arrangements to meet all these requirements. It is our assumption that key issues in connection with this case will be raised in the month of March. I am referring to experts whose expert opinions you have had occasion to read, as well as some of the key witnesses which are material to this case. We believe that these key testimonies could be shifted by your decision. This is the minimum of time that we need in order to arrange these things. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Actually, when Mr. Petrovic raised this to me, his comment was: We need a few days. It was not a week. The only comment that the Prosecution could make was that we have witnesses scheduled through the end of February, and we are hopeful that if it moves along with due speed, that these witnesses will be able to arrive and testify and go home. Our -- as the Chamber knows, VWU, we don't want to bring people here, having returned not testified. So as it stands the schedule is made with arrivals scheduled for, I think it's up to 27th, 28th February. So literally the end of the month. If the Chamber feels -- and I'd want to make it a matter of record, we do not want to see the accused deprived of family visits. This is never something that we think should be the case in normal circumstances. If the Chamber is persuaded that the Defence has made out cause, then we leave it certainly in the Chamber's hands, but we were talking about a few days as opposed to a week. We are mindful that some of the heaviest witnesses will be coming in the month of March, and it is going to be a very - for lack of a better word - brutal trial schedule with heavy examination, including former co-accused, experts, significant political. So we are working at the same difficult pace that the Chamber and the Defence and the accused are working at. If the Chamber nonetheless sees that there is a place for the request, then again, we had looked at it as a few days, but we leave it -- we understand that there could be a time consequence if it went beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, looking ahead and without seeking any binding commitment or observation from you, if according to the present pace we reach the end of February with the witnesses, can you give some indication to the Chamber when the expert witnesses on which you are relying are likely to be called in March. Will they be early in the month, middle of the month or late in the month?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: They would be late in the month, Your Honour. They would be toward the end. Strategically placed and also by virtue of the time limits that are required by the Rules unless there is any waiver of such, which I would not anticipate. But toward the end of the month. And again, the list of witnesses is heavy. I would anticipate significant cross-examination of these witnesses as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But -- yes, very well. I was going to make a light comment then, but I've changed my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: But does that answer your question, though, generally about the placement of them, toward the end of the month. Certainly the initial time frame that everyone contemplated a different pace of examination. That has not materialised. I think we have all had to work accordingly. But given the situation in the courtroom, it would appear that -- end of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And how do you see the time which we will needed for the Prosecution case at present?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Because they are coming at the end of March, depending on cross-examination, I suppose literally end of March or first week or weeks into April I would say that finishing. Realistically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that take into account the need for a week? Or if there were a week, would that need to be added on to your estimate?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think that would be adding on to it, and additionally depending on the medical issues, that will not be -- that's a hearing that I assume would be taking several days. And that's an additional expert realm of testimony that neither -- well, certainly the Prosecution did not contemplate when it set out its schedule. So I think that would be my response. We're looking at additional to -- plus anything that comes out of the medical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So if we were to grant this application, we would be extending the trial by that time and with the need also to consider medical, we could well be to the mid of April before we finish the Prosecution case on present indications.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think that is entirely realistic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've taken up nearly an hour and ten minutes of the session. The Chamber would propose to have the morning break now and to give consideration to this application and resume again at half past for two longer sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With regard to the matter raised just before the adjournment, we've been persuaded that some break in the proceedings is justified. But given the total programme of the trial and the other commitments that have to be considered, the first week in March is not one that is terribly convenient. What we have in mind is that there should be a break commencing with Thursday the 11th of March, which is toward the end of the second week of March, with a resumption then on Thursday the 18th of March. That will allow not only a full week but a weekend, and it will fit in, we think, a little better with the progress of the trial. It will be before the experts come to give evidence for the Prosecution. It will fit better with the timetable for the medical review of the health of the accused. And we therefore propose that in your planning of evidence, Ms. Somers, you should be sure that a witness finishes on the 10th or else is a witness who can readily return. Will that be adequate for your needs, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just ask one more bit in aid of the medical aspect. We are anticipating full cooperation from the Detention Unit based on the consent of General Strugar to have access to his records. Should there be any need for further order for copying, for example, of any type of film or record, if I may simply submit a copy through the normal channels to the Chamber. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we may be able to turn to Mr. Kaufman's witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kaiser. I'm sorry that we were delayed this morning on other issues. Could I remind you of the affirmation you took when your evidence commenced, which is still applicable. Yes, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: If it pleases Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kaiser, thank you very much for returning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Usher, before you sit down if the bundles that we had open yesterday could be placed once again in front of the witness, that is the bundles containing the witness's exhibits. Your Honours, whilst the bundles are being placed in front of Dr. Kaiser, perhaps it would be appropriate to say that the Prosecution will adopt the same procedure that has been adopted in matters of other bundles which have been placed in front of witnesses such that if there are documents which are not referred to by the witness during his testimony, then of course, those documents will be removed form the bundles. I should like to add furthermore that there will be perhaps a couple of documents in these bundles which would better be addressed by a witness who is scheduled to appear not next week but the week after, Mr. Janicot who is also a UNESCO official. I should add furthermore that there are a number of legal documents which I would submit are matters of judicial notice, and in any event contained in these bundles. In this matter, I indicate that there are two conventions at least contained in the bundle, and those are for Your Honours' convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's very helpful. Thank you, Mr. Kaufman. And if as we progress through the bundles you can indicate the documents which are better addressed by the witness to come, it will facilitate our grasp of that matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. That is what I, in fact, propose to do, first of all, with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: If we may start. Dr. Kaiser, you now have the bundles in front of you. Could you perhaps open up the first bundle to tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness will not refer to tab 1. This will be a matter better dealt with by, as I said, Mr. Janicot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: But Dr. Kaiser, document number 2 -- tab 2. I believe you have the wrong bundle open in front of you. Is that tab 2, sir? I believe you have the wrong bundle. It's the larger of the two.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't recall seeing any tabs in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Oh. I apologise. No, you have -- I believe the wrong bundles have been placed in front of the witness. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could be of assistance. I wonder whether, Your Honours, this would be an appropriate time for the bundles to be assigned at least a number, to avoid future confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, they will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P63.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Kaiser, document number 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bearing in mind the discussion we had when we addressed this topic the last time, with respect to the report on the damage, at the end of the cross-examination of the witness, I ask that everything be marked for identification only. And then at the end of the examination, we shall be able to see what is and what is not an exhibit. The same profile of documents is before you in this case as in the previous case, which is why I request that the formal admission of the documents be delayed until the end of the examination, and that they be marked for identification purposes only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was acting on the basis that had been indicated by Mr. Kaufman, that while a number has been allocated only those documents actually referred to and identified by the witness would remain in the bundle. But my instincts are with you, Mr. Petrovic, and we will have this marked for identification as 63 for the moment. And if there is any issue at the end of the evidence of the witness, it can be considered. But no doubt some of the bundle, if not all of it, will become Exhibit P63. But for the moment, marked for identification, P63.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, tab 2. Are you familiar with this document? You mentioned yesterday that you were familiar with Dubrovnik's UNESCO status. Perhaps you could enlighten to us what this is.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the nomination submitted by the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for submission of the Old Town of Dubrovnik on the World Heritage List.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So are you able to expand upon the nature of the World Heritage List, or would you rather that that be left to Mr. Janicot?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked with the questions related to the World Heritage List when I was the director of international council of monuments and sites. Because ICOMOS was an institutional partner which was asked for its opinion about the nominations. And ICOMOS would ask a consultant to examine the nomination according to the different criteria. I have not worked with criteria and these documents for a very long time. I could answer some questions about Dubrovnik. But I wouldn't feel comfortable to deal with this very sort of old matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, the documents are self-explanatory and I would submit that they will be the subject of legal discussion at a later date in any event. But are you aware of the dates upon which, or the year at any rate on which the Old Town Dubrovnik was inscribed on the World Heritage List?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, moving on to the next document at tab 3 and tab 4, at some stage I believe there was an expansion of the Old Town of Dubrovnik. Perhaps you could enlighten us as to that. This concerns documents 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say about this is first of all it gives me a certain amount of pleasure that see that in 1993 there was an extension of the World Heritage Site, because in our mission report for the mission of November/December 1991, in annex 16 of that report, we drew attention to certain, let's say, inconsistencies in the nomination, the argument being that the nomination did not fully cover the traditional urban system of the Old Town of Dubrovnik. And I was very pleased to discover very recently that in fact the Republic of Croatia had made such a demand too for the extension of the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to tax you too much with perhaps details that you're not familiar with offhand, because as I say it's all contained in the document at any rate. But are you familiar in what way the Old Town of Dubrovnik was expanded for the purposes of an amendment, addition inclusion on the World Heritage List?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the original nomination gave us the limits of the nomination site, the walls of the Old Town and the ditches. But there were other features. It wasn't clear to us, for example, if the Old Port was included because it was just outside the walls. It wasn't on the other side of a ditch. There was a question of the breakwater, the kasa [phoen] which was very old which -- mediaeval structure. There were quarantine buildings which were east of Dubrovnik, which was very, very important because this was where the merchandise was brought and kept for a certain period of time. We also raised -- drew attention to the site of the lazareto which is where people would be if they are suspected of being ill they would be kept. And that was all part of the urban economy and the management of the city. I think maybe we mentioned Revelin which was an outer work on the east side of Dubrovnik. And then there was the fortress Lovrijenac which was to the west, which struck us as being part of what we -- a defence system of the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Moving on to tab 5 we see the letter that was to you yesterday. That being, as you explained in your evidence yesterday, your mandate, as it were. After that letter there is a document, a rather substantial document, which will form the large part of your evidence today. Could you briefly in a few words explain what that was. We'll go into a detail -- in detail at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the mission report that was done by Mr. Carnez and myself, following our mission to Dubrovnik in November and December 1991. I can go into great detail about different components of it and different objectives, purposes, of the report if the Court so wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, we will do that in due course, Dr. Kaiser. For the time being we're just going through the bundle so the Court is aware of what are contained in these bundles for future reference. So perhaps if we could now move on to the second bundle. And tab 6. I think this is fairly self-explanatory, but this is a UNESCO document entitled "Properties Inscribed on the World Heritage List." Yes, that's the document. What do we have here?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This simply appears to be a list of properties that were parts of -- were listed properties on the World Heritage List as of July 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And on page 3, the Old City of Dubrovnik is inscribed, along with a number of other sites in Croatia. Tab 7, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I believe that a confusion has arisen as to the tabs, because I'm informed by Ms. McCreath that we have tabs that are numbered 8 and tabs that are numbered 7 for this particular document. The document I am referring to is a document -- the second document in the second bundle. And the document is entitled "Establishment of the World Heritage List." Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: General principles, Dr. Kaiser, are you able to enlighten us on these, what this is?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is kind of a framework document for deciding what the World Heritage List will be about. But as I said earlier, this is the type of material I have been away from for a very, very long. This is kind of a guidebook, a framework for the principles, probably criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on. The next document is a document written in French and in English. Translation is supplied. It's entitled "1991-1992 Biens culturels endommages lors des bombardements", "cultural properties damaged by shelling, 1991 to 1992." This is a UNESCO report as well, is it?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact this is the UNESCO programme for the restoration of cultural properties which had been damaged in the bombardments in 1991 and 1992. This was prepared by UNESCO in cooperation with the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Heritage of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the documents that remain in the bundles are legal documents, two conventions, which are the subject -- one of which at any rate is the subject matter of this -- the indictment, counts 4 to 6, and ratification documents. But I shan't trouble the witness with these documents. As I say they are purely legal documents and will be addressed, no doubt, in submissions to the Court at a later stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kaiser, for your assistance in that matter. Now, if we can turn back to where we left off yesterday, as it were the narrative. But before we do that, I have one clarification question. You mentioned a meeting with a colonel by the name of Stamenkovic. Just so it's clear for the record, Stamenkovic was associated with which organisation, which body?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the liaison officer with the 5th Military District, therefore in contact with various organisations, international community organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So yesterday you talked about implementing the plan for verifying the damage that had been done in the months of October and November 1991. Now, please remind us, your role there was as a consultant. What would you do to verify that damage? What administrative aids would you use for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally there should be some sort of reporting format that exists for damage. There of course are reporting formats all over the world, administrations, companies, et cetera, et cetera. The question here was that this was a matter of war damage. There did not seem to be any particular available reporting format. There would be reporting formats later on in Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, which were basically adaptations of damage surveys, adapted to war damage. And -- but in Dubrovnik we found that there was no particular available reporting format that seemed to be adequate. When I went back through my report, I found that there was an allusion to a reporting format for the earthquake of 1979 which apparently -- I can't remember the reasons why we thought that was not adequate. So it was very, very important to establish a methodology and a form which would help to guarantee consistency in our reports. And I think that after the first one or two sites that we happened to see I sat down and I drew up a reporting format.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: In that matter, may I ask you to look at your monitor. Perhaps if you could press the button entitled "video," we will show you an image, "video evidence," please. Do you have a document displayed on your screen?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps if you could enlighten us to that particular document. What is that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the particular form that I drew up. It's in French because it was a bilingual mission. My partner in the mission was a Francophone. So this was a French language form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So kindly take us through this fiche and translate it for the benefit of those of us who are not familiar with the French language.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Degats de guerre a Dubrovnik", that's war damage in Dubrovnik. "Fiche", that's the form, that was for the number of the form. "Numero de l'Institut", this was a reference to the number that the institute itself had put on their preliminary damage assessment. "Date et heure de releve", that is the date, the time that the survey was made. "Localisation", this is the address of the structure of the building, whatever it was. This "Structure" was the what -- whether it was a house, whether it was a fountain, whether it was a church. "Date presume des degats", this is the presumed date of the damage. "Projectile", that of course is the projectile. It was very important that we find the projectile. After all, We are supposed to be looking at war damage. "Description des degats", description of the damage, which is simply what was the condition of the particular structure, or part of the structure when we saw it. "Appreciation des desgats", this was sort of a -- an evaluation of the damage in terms of its importance. "Divers", miscellaneous. "Comparison avec appreciation de l'Institut", this is simply a comparison with the comments that had been made by the institute in their preliminary assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, in the evidence of a previous witness, we discussed what would become known as categories of damage. Had that system of classification been introduced when you were doing your examinations in the months -- concerning the months of October and November?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had not introduced that -- this sort of notation or damage in the earlier assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what happened on your first foray into the Old Town in pursuance of this mission?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first foray was in the Stradun and the first building that we visited was a house on Boskoviceva Street where there had been a number of impacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what -- on what date those impacts were caused?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the annex 3 of the report I mention some dates. I think that those dates for that particular house, I think it had been struck on the 23rd of October in the shellings in November from the 10th to 12th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Did you meet the occupant of that particular address?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I met the -- I met an older woman who was cleaning her house out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: What did she tell you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she laughed and said, They always hit us here, in this house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, please, sir, describe the damage that you encountered on Boskoviceva Street on your first foray into the Old town, from that building to the surrounding buildings.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this particular building which was on the corner, Boskoviceva Street and the Stradun, had been hit in the roof, so it presented roof damage. It appears -- the roof tiles had gone out. Part of the roof was open to the sky. It was -- at the top of the building I had actually pulled out a projectile. This was the first projectile I had seen in fact in situ. There was also another -- a direct impact on the east facade of that house, not at street level but quite high up. And as for the surrounding houses, the surrounding houses, of course, presented some damage which came from shrapnel -- well, which is to say it could have come from roof tiles blown off the roof, or in the case of this big impact which was on the wall, it could come from the fragments of the shell or from the stone that was damaged. A lot of windows were blown out. I can't remember in great detail what each of those houses opposite the house on -- the damaged house -- exactly what the damage was, but it's in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And as you mentioned, that is contained in annex 3 to your report, which is to be found at tab 5 of the bundles we've placed in front of Their Honours. Now, sir, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies for interrupting my learned friend and the witness, Your Honour. Unfortunately I'm not able to find annex 3 in my copy of the document. I've looked at both English and French version of the text and I seem unable to locate annex 3 at tab 6. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: If I may assist Mr. Petrovic in this matter. This, Mr. Petrovic, was the document that was passed to you at the beginning of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it not in the bundle?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I believe it is in Your Honours' bundles. It might not necessarily be in Mr. Petrovic's bundle because we gave him advanced copies of these exhibits so he could prepare himself as appropriate for the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. If this is indeed the case. My apologies to both my learned friend and the Trial Chamber. I don't have it here right now, but I will have a look in my files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm still finding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, Your Honours, it does not have a cover sheet marked "annex 3," it is actually marked annex 3 on the document itself, in -- the body of the document in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have found it. It's page 607 of the last numerals. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, I would like to clarify your last answer, Dr. Kaiser. You mentioned that you pulled a projectile out of that particular building. What did you actually pull out. Could you be more specific.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a metal cylinder about this length. And at the end of the metal cylinder, there were a lot of little aluminum tails, like little wings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the record, I think by your hand you indicated something like 10 centimetres, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I have never been very good at assessing distances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Don't rely on me, Mr. Kaufman, but we have the witness's concurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the address, sir? I will ask you to draw it on the map that we had put in front of you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps if that could be placed in front of the witness once again. With the blue felt tip, if you could perhaps mark the position of the house. Please draw a box.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the number of that house?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And the damage to the surrounding houses, perhaps if you could put a few dots on the -- without drawing any circles or anything, just a few dots where the damage was incurred to surrounding houses.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So I take it, sir, that you continued in this activity until the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Please tell the Court where you were on the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was in the institute, because the institute is where we were lodged. I was in my bed early in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And how were you woken up?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was woken up by a great deal of racket, explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember at what time this was?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 5.48 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: How can you be so sure? 5.48 is a fairly accurate time, if I may say. One is normally -- may say ten to 6.00, or quarter to 6.00. But you say 5.48? How do you know 5.48?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe my watch was wrong, but that's what was on my watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, you say "racket," what type of racket?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of explosions that I could hear, a large number of explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And judging by the acoustics, do you know where those explosions where coming from in relation to where you were positioned?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those explosions seemed to be coming from up on the ridge north of Dubrovnik, Srdj, the Srdj area. It's a general area which I'm referring to. It's not possible to say exactly what point on the ridge, but they were coming from -- to the left of where I was standing, and they seemed to be up on the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Did those explosions, acoustics which you're describing remain statically positioned or did they change at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an extremely strange aural effect after about 10 or 20 minutes after I had been -- I was standing there in the workroom listening to this. And about 10 to 20 minutes afterwards all of a sudden there was, like -- it all shifted. And the explosions were very, very close and they seemed more to be around us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, you were in the Old Town, so to where had the acoustics shifted geographically?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seemed to me that there was shooting on the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So you mentioned the word "shooting," please -- is that the word?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard in fact were explosions and explosions and explosions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So what did you do because of that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think to -- after I got over the initial surprise, it became quite apparent that this was dangerous. So we -- there were three other people. There was Mr. Carnez and then there was a cafe owner who had come to see how we were and there was Mr. Franic who crossed town, because as he said what were these two international people going to do under these conditions. There were four of us. We went down to the toilets which were not a whole level down but sort of a mezzanine at the rear of the building and we took shelter in the toilets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Had the sun risen at that stage, sir? Was it light of day or was it still dark?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the shutters of the buildings were always closed at night and we had left the shutters closed. So there was no light at that point except when we got into the toilets. I cannot remember exactly the light -- the light was there, but it was morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You mean by that, light of day, do you, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Light of day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: How long were you in the toilets seeking refuge?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't there very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was right opposite the window. The toilets had a window. And all of a sudden there was a big flash, an orange flash, on the wall of a house just behind the institute. And it of course occurred to me it was an extremely dangerous place because we might be hit by shrapnel and something like that. And I simply pushed everybody out of the toilets. And we went down to the ground floor level.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You mention orange flash. Was there any sound accompanying that orange flash?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was -- there were lots and lots of noises at that time. I remember, above all, the big orange flash. I don't remember the noise from that particular impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So you sought alternate refuge. Where was that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the entrance of the institute, as I said, on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So how long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very long. Ten minutes, something like that. There were glass windows, of course, at the entrance, and there was of course a physical -- there is a very particular type of physical feeling when there is so much noise going on. And one of great, let's say, fragility. I remember feeling very much afraid of something coming through the window and the window coming with it, and the glass coming with it. So we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went up in the Dominican Monastery which was just on the other side running around the cloister. And entering -- so we were in the north wing, and we were, not at ground level, but there was a level below the ground level, which is where I spent most of the rest of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, you've talked about explosions and acoustics that you heard of those explosions. For how long did those explosions continue, the explosions that you heard in the early hours of the morning?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a lot of shooting it seemed, a lot of explosions, for a couple of hours. It's a little -- I wasn't watching my watch throughout that period. But there was -- there were a lot of explosions and it went on for several hours in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps you could estimate a time, if possible.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say about two and a half hours to three hours, starting from the beginning of this bombardment, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, was that intensity of shelling maintained throughout the day?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't, it wasn't maintained throughout the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Please tell the Chamber when the intensity of the shelling changed?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was this initial of what seemed to be very long period of intense shelling. And then that began to die down later in the morning with more interspersed kinds of shelling, but less in intensity. And around 11.00, 11.30, there was a really rapid decrease in shelling to very little, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: At what time did you notice that the shelling had stopped in toto, if it may be said?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was later on because there was periodic shells that were falling. And 3.00, 3.30, something like that time, there was no more shelling at all. It was completely quiet, totally silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And just so it's clear for the record, are we talking about matters that you conclude on the basis of hearing or on the basis of seeing?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is really on the basis of hearing, not seeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, what was Mr. Carnez doing at this moment in time throughout the day?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically we were all together huddled with the -- a certain number of the inhabitants of the monastery. Mr. Carnez was, however, able to get through to Paris on a telephone that the monastery had which was functioning. And he was able to speak with the -- Mr. Janicot, Mr. Vogric, and of course with the director general of UNESCO, Mr. Mayor himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: By "Paris," you mean UNESCO headquarters?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: When did you come out of your shelter on that day?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I came out to see the church in the early afternoon, I came out of the Dominican Monastery when night had fallen. There was a question that there was a great deal of wind. We knew that there had been damage because Mr. Carnez and Mr. Franic had gone out about the same time that as I went to visit the church, and there was concern that the wind the Bora would in fact spread the fire from building to building. So I went out with Mr. Franic to see what the -- what was going on, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You mentioned the wind and you gave it a name, the Bora. Perhaps you could enlighten us as to this term. Which type of wind does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a cold mountain wind that blows along the Neretva. There are a couple of winds in the area, there is the Sirocco and then there is also the Bora. They are very strong winds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Did you survey the Old Town that night, the night of the 6th?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course it was dark. What I was able -- what we were able to do is approach those buildings that were still burning and there were a number of them that were still burning. And in fact the fire department was fighting the fire on one -- in one of the buildings which was in the Sirocco. I also went into a house - it was in fact Mr. Vetma's house in the town - and was able to see the inter-university centre which was burning at that time. I saw the house called Zarokom. It's not a palace, not a great house, but I saw the house in flames with its owner standing in front of it. I could see the fires -- some fire - we didn't get very close - of other buildings that were on Od Puca Street and then we went back. There were a lot of things coming off the roofs too. It was very unpleasant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: This was all in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Let's turn to the following day, the 7th of December. Tell us what you did on the morning of the 7th of December.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the morning of the 7th of December we, like everybody else, went out to see what the town looked like. So we were in the morning simply walking around, getting a first visual impression of what Dubrovnik was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Did you see any evidence of human injury that morning?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any evidence of human injury, physical human injury, that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, from information already before the Trial Chamber, we know that a detailed survey of the damage to the Old Town was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: That's -- for the benefit of Trial Chamber is P51 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us how it came about that that detailed survey was instituted.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went out on the 7th of December in the morning, it was very, very clear, just visually, that there had been a lot of damage done. It didn't bear any resemblance to what I had -- we had seen in terms of damage that was done in October and November a great deal. The director-general wanted to know quickly what the extent of that damage was, and it was something that we would have to report on to him. And it's not something that one team can do beginning in the afternoon of the 7th and also on the 8th, we would -- we had two small teams. There was Mr. Carnez who went with Mr. Vetma in the north half of the town and I went with Mr. Franic in the south half of the town. And we had to send information quickly back to the director-general, so we did what I would call a spot survey. And the map of this survey is in fact -- is contained in our report. And that developed a sense of the extent of damage in the town, and of course convinced me that all of -- our mission was to be there another two weeks. It was absolutely impossible for us to get a real grasp of the damage by ourselves. It was imperative -- because we believed that UNESCO would make a commitment to the restoration of the town, it was imperative to try to organise the information on the damage to the town which would help to direct UNESCO and teams of experts who would come afterwards to deal with the restoration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Just for the benefit of the transcript and the Trial Chamber. That spot assessment which you carried out on the 7th, that is contained, as you say, in the annex to your report at tab 5. It is annex 4A, I believe. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, a perusal of that map will show a basic, if I may say, methodology. Did you refine your methodology at any stage?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some refinements carried out if you look at this map and if you look at later maps of -- well, that's presentations, in fact.
