Presentation changed a little bit from that particular map to maps that were carried out and drawn up later on. At that time there was the question of trying -- because we realised we were -- as I mentioned before, we realised we were in the face of danger, that damage that was really very extensive damage. So we were looking for scales of helping to draw the attention of the teams to things and we thought would be a priority matter in a way that would help them get to the heart of the matter. So this is where the question of the so-called scale of damage emerged. It was right around this time that we began thinking about some sort of scale or different categories of damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, as we will later see, you settled on four categories of damage classification, and also there was devised a system of identifying types of damage as opposed to assessment of damage. Now, before we move on you mentioned that you split up the Old Town in your first forays into the Old Town after the 6th of December into north and south. What was the dividing line?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dividing line was simply the Stradun for that first, preliminary survey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, let us move on to the categories of damage. Categories 1, 2, 3, and 4 which appear in the preliminary report prepared by the Institute for the Protection of Monuments in Dubrovnik. Who devised these categories of damage: One, two, three, and four?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I devised that categorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Would you like to expand upon that, on what basis you devised them?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I explained earlier, we were looking for something which would help to focus the interest and the work of later teams. There were four categories or types of damage. And it's important to realise that these are types of damage more than real assessment of degree of damage. It was a little bit mixed. Category 1 was simply the buildings that had been burned out. Category 2 was structures that had been hit on the roof and also on the facades. Category 3 was structures which had been hit on the roof or the facades. And category 4 was very, very light damage, which is basically damage from shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, in the preliminary report there are also a number of symbols. We have black triangles, we have black dots, white triangles, as it were. Could you explain those symbols and who devised them.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the black dot was inspired simply because of the very first preliminary survey which the locals had done, they used black dots for everything. A black dot was an impact on a stone facade, a stone surface, such as the Stradun, the pavement. So that was a black dot. A black triangle was a direct impact upon a roof. Then there was a white triangle which was simply the fragments, the secondary damage, which would be done on a roof from fragments. There was also fully filled-in black square which was a building, which followed the contours of the building. Then there was sort of -- not really a double line, but a thicker line for buildings that had been partially burned out. Then there were also dots that we used along the fronts of buildings to indicate that this was an area in fact which had been damaged by fragments. I think that's an exhaustive description of the different symbols that we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Were these symbols unique or have you come across them in your prior experience as a UNESCO or ICOMOS employee?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen symbols like this and I did see them -- I saw them later on. I remember seeing some reports of damage from the city of Sarajevo in 1992, which in fact had adopted at least part of the -- some of the symbols.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: To your knowledge, has this methodology ever been adopted in the past or is it likely to be adopted in the future?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This methodology is an improvisation. It served -- it was a certain purpose that it had to serve. As I said, it was not an assessment of the degree of damage. It was a way of providing information and guidance for the future. I have no idea what has been done in the -- after that in particular circumstances. I was in other places during the wars, I was in Croatia and then I was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And for example in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Mostar at the end of 1992. A very capable institute. The people in fact were starting to use a damage classification analysis system which was being used, in fact, in Zagreb, but which I think had been taken simply as common throughout the former Yugoslavia. But dots and squares and triangles of buildings following bombardments, I don't think I have seen this since.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You distinguished between direct impacts and what you call secondary damage in one of your previous answers. How would you go about doing that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a direct impact creates a crater of some size, of some width, and some depth, and will vary with the type of ordinance that's being used. And where you see traces where there is this crater, and it's usually some sort of circular or variant form, that is a direct impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: If you didn't see the circular form that you described, then you would register it, I assume, as an indirect impact?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's another question about the roofs, because it's a little bit more complicated. A crater on a stone facade or on the stone pavement is pretty clear. The question of a direct impact on a roof is something different. You have to judge it partly because of what you find, if you find the traces of the projectile very close to the main damage, and also the extent of the damage to the roof. That kind of damage -- there is no crater on the roof, because whenever it hits it, it usually goes through. The indirect damage is different. It's simply the result of -- either of a blast effect against windows, against walls as well. Or as a question simply shrapnel which has been scattered around and which can break up tiles very easily and can break windows and can put holes in walls, holes in doors, and scratches on stone walls. And that's -- this is indirect damage -- indirect impact, no indirect damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You mention that there were approximately four of you who set out to do a preliminary survey of the damage caused by the shelling of the 6th of December. And you split yourselves up between the north part of the town and the southern part of the town. Did the number of people working on this project increase at any stage?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it increased very considerably. We could not -- we had to list as much of the -- well, in fact we listed all of the institute members for the survey and there were even some volunteer architects from some other institutes or from private practice who even joined the teams. The methodology was the same, but the organisation of the survey was rather different. I mean, we had -- there was a division into districts of the Old Town of Dubrovnik. I believe that this division had actually been used in looking at the 1979 earthquake damage, and so a team would be assigned to a district and they would go with the form -- of course, we explained everything to them. But there were a lot more people involved in the full survey than in the little surveys that we were carrying out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: This division into subdistricts, would that be the insulae?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be insulae.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You say you would explain to them what to do. Now I take it you were the person who did the explaining and Carnez by -- or you said the plural?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did most of the explaining because I carried -- I had actually carried out mainly the surveys in October and November. And so I explained the and I developed the form. So I did most of the explaining. And because these people of course had not worked -- there were only two people who worked with us on the early survey, so they had to be informed about how to do it. They also had to be informed also about such questions as projectiles. There were a couple of explaining sessions, I remember, and then also as the work went on, we would come in at the end of the day. So there was some sort of guidance that continued for the two weeks that we were there until our return to Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You mentioned the word "guidance." Would it therefore be correct to state that you had guidance over this project?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think guidance is the best way to describe it. It wasn't that every single -- we were -- it was guidance, because in the two weeks after the bombardment we were so solicited by headquarters for other matters about Dubrovnik, preliminary estimates of damage -- preliminary -- trying to put figures together, how much money, things like that; drawing up the priorities for intervention; and then we had delegation after delegation of journalists. It was really quite a -- it was quite a circus. I shouldn't say that, but it was very, very, very demanding. So we gave guidance. We didn't verify everything that was going on because we simply didn't have the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Annex 7 to your report which you prepared -- we will discuss when you submitted your report at a later stage. But annex 7 shows some statistics which seem to have been submitted by the Institute for the Protection of Monuments in Dubrovnik. Do you accept those statistics by virtue of their incorporation into your report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I accept those statistics. The only slight qualification is that it was still ongoing work. But they were very, very good statistics. I was very -- in fact I was very -- I later on saw, I was pretty proud of the work that they had done and I accept those statistics, but I qualify them that they would change a little bit after that for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: So by virtue of the fact that you say there was still ongoing work, you accept that these statistics were the result of the preliminary survey, the preliminary report, which is marked P51 MFI?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, on the 7th of December, did you have occasion to meet Matko Vetma?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I had occasion to meet Matko Vetma on the 7th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Did any of you have any contacts with JNA officials that day?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vetma in fact did meet a delegation that came from the federal army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Enlighten the Trial Chamber please, sir, as to what you know about that particular meeting and Mr. Vetma's reaction thereto.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had returned to the institute in the early part of the afternoon, and Mr. Vetma was not there. And he joined us later. And he was rather white -- he was white-faced. I think he was upset and he said: They came to see the town. And I said, What do you mean they came to see the town? He said: The federal army came to see the town and I guided them around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Whilst we're on the subject of JNA officials and/or soldiers, did you have occasion to witness any JNA officials or soldiers whilst you were in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during one of the trips up to the Hotel Argentina, which is where the UNICEF offices were and the ECMM were also based there, on one occasion I saw soldiers walking from Zarkovica towards Mount Srdj. There were four of them. They were walking in an Indian file. I don't know how many metres they were apart from each other. That's the only time I saw any soldiers whom I thought were from the federal forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, there are a number of maps in your report, and your report deals with damage that occurred in October and November, by virtue of annex 3. How can you give us an indication of filtering out damage that occurred in October and November from damage that occurred in December? I ask you this question because the matter has arisen that during the preparation of the survey, damage which was incurred in November might have been confused with damage which was caused in December. So if you could, assist us in that filtering process.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the big damage survey which was carried out, they -- you will find mentions made of damage, the dates the damage was carried out. So the person who filled out the form was aware that there was a layering of damage, in fact. That should be kept in mind. The second point to be kept in mind is that in fact sometime -- sometime after our own report was prepared, that elements of it were sent -- were given to the people on the ground. So they had seen the damage, they had recorded what they had seen, including when -- of course when it had happened; and they also had other means of checking -- when the damage -- what was the cause, when it was, et cetera. It wasn't so difficult to separate this damage out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And your annex 3, that listed damage incurred in what month?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The annex 3 listed damage done in October and November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Was that report before the Institute for the Protection of Monuments at any stage, before the officials there?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you remember -- I am a consultant. I worked on the report. I submitted my report, and then I didn't work anymore on Dubrovnik. And then UNESCO was charged with transmitting those documents -- or what parts of those documents that they wanted to do. There were parts of the report, notably -- the conclusions were for the director-general. I don't know if those conclusions were transmitted, but many things were transmitted. For example, I mentioned earlier the annex 16 was also transmitted and it gave rise to the extension of the World Heritage Site. Colleagues from UNESCO transmitted the necessary information to the institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sorry, I should have been more clear in my question. Annex 3 to your report, the annex which you state has a description of the damage which you noticed having occurred in October and November, was that before the institute when they prepared their preliminary report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because when they were preparing their preliminary report, they were preparing it in December and January, which is -- the reports are being prepared at the same time. My report would have been available to them after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: My last question on annex 3. Annex 3 was prepared on the basis of information you had received. What information was that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Annex 3 was prepared on the basis of my own survey carried out in October and November. There was a preliminary report that they had done for these little shellings, and they had used that as a guide. But my report was a separate thing. My report was the verification of the damage on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I'd like to look at some of the projectiles listed in your preliminary report -- sorry, in the preliminary report, being projectiles I would assume that you found as well. This is to be found in P51 marked for identification. But for convenience's sake I have marked the relevant page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps if Mr. Usher could distribute this. This item is to be found in bundle 1 of P51 MFI. Its number is ERN 01069068.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, could you take us through these items.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this thing at the top is a 62-millimetre mortar. I never saw one of these in situ in Dubrovnik, although some of them had been picked up, but where I don't know. This is a small mortar. It's an 82-millimetre mortar. There were a lot of these on the 6th of December, and there were none before that I was able to pick up. These were picked up in situ.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Item number 3.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that we called a rocket. I'm not an expert, but -- and it's not exactly the one that we picked up in Dubrovnik. What was similar is the cylinder, although this is a cylinder that has bars -- rings around it, and ours didn't really have that. However, this little tail is very, very, very close to the tail that we found on the similar projectiles in Dubrovnik, 82-millimetre --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Calibre --

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Projectile, calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: The next one down, item 4.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one particularly is a 120-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And did you find items like that in Dubrovnik in the conduct of the survey?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the survey before -- that is tails. This is the part that would come off here and sometimes fragments. This we encountered few in the shellings that had taken place before the 6th of December and a lot on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And finally, number 5. Yes, the last item on that page.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a Malyutka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: What's a Malyutka?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a wire-guided rocket. This is -- I can show you the wire here at the end. What we saw in Dubrovnik from this was basically the tail end which consisted of the mechanism, the engines that are the driving the thing, also a great deal of wire coiled around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, now I would like to take you to the ramparts of the Old Town of Dubrovnik. This, once again, is contained in the first bundle of P51 MFI, but for the sake of convenience I have reproduced it in a single-page format. Here we see the Old Town of Dubrovnik on a map. Could you enlighten to us what you see with respect to the ramparts in this map.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see these dots and the dots represent the impacts upon the ramparts. And you can see that there is a certain number of dots which are on the Fort St. John down here on the kasa here, the breakwater. Along the front here of the Old Port. And then there is a series of impacts along the north wall here. Some of those are in fact -- well, you can see quite clearly that there seem to be a lot which are inside the ramparts and here on the west wall down to Pile gate, a similar situation. And along the sea wall front, there is virtually nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Just for demonstration purpose, if you could point to the direction of Zarkovica on that map. Just put your pointer on the map, if you could, and show us where Zarkovica would be.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you had an opportunity to tour the ramparts?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Did you tour the ramparts after the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And would that map, to the best of my knowledge, accurately reflect what you saw on the ramparts?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: We've now talked about walls and we've talked about the tail fins of projectiles. Did you have occasion to see the tail fin -- tail fins of projectiles in situ?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. There were -- there was a certain number of tail fins which were in situ, in walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Can you remember any particular instances of tail fins of projectiles which you found embedded in walls?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the earlier shellings I remember a tail fin which was in the Sponza Palace, the east wall. I remember a tail fin which was on St. John Bastion facing eastward, which was on the rear windows, and it was embedded on a wall. In a house which is behind -- that is, to the west of the Dominican Monastery, again this is shelling before the 6th of December, I remember a tail fin in a wall, because I remember a Macedonian soldier who was a member of the Croatian defence forces, I remember him pulling it out of the wall. Cause I had gone in to see what -- if it had gone through, and of course it had actually gone -- it has pushed the mortar through. I remember a tail fin in the west wall of the city but the inner wall behind the old -- the old folks' home, and that was in the wall blow the parapet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You said the old folks' home. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dom Staraca. It was it was in fact the hospice, it was for citizens in the third age.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I interrupted you. I do apologise. That was in the wall below the parapet?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, before I ask you a question about those tail fins embedded in walls, perhaps it would be a good opportunity to show you something, to show you a photograph. This is to be found in P51 MFI. In the B/C/S version which is the one which contains the photographs, 01069130.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I am afraid I do not have a single copy of this to hand out, because I fear if I were to photocopy it then the quality would be even less than it is at present. But perhaps if that bundle can be placed in front of the witness, and I would request that the witness comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: It should be marked 01069130 at the top. Sir, do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here is the tail fin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And where is that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in the little port near the jetty. That's after the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And that is a tail fin, is it, embedded in the wall as you described?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, bear that tail fin in mind and the other tail fins that you've described that you saw in the aftermath of the 6th of December. Trace a line back, perpendicularly if you can, from the tail fin. In which direction would that be? Where would that be coming from?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be coming from an easterly direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Would there be any particular geographical feature in that easterly direction?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Zarkovica is in an easterly direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. Now, this time we do have the benefit of modern technology in order to display a colour photograph to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Sir, please, if you could have a look at your monitor now. Press the button "video evidence." Now, what do we see in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we see a shop on the Stradun, which has been damaged by shelling. And we see shrapnel damage, and we also see an orangish-brownish-reddish stain on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: What can you tell us about that orange-brown stain on the wall?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we thought that this came from a marking mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Why do you say "we thought"? On what do you base this?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had had a -- there was a certain number of conversations we had about shells. Sometimes people like the French military from the hospital ship -- sometimes there were local people. And the -- in some conversations, some discussion, the fact that marking mortars could be used came up. And there were a certain number of impacts in which this kind of stain was evident after the 6th of December. There was even one before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: What do you understand by the term, sir, "marking mortar"?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I understand by the term "marking mortar" is a shell that is put in to make a great deal of smoke in order to indicate to other artillery where they should fire. It can be used for hiding things as well. But marking is especially, I think, for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Do you know what the chemical composition is of the material that causes the staining on the wall?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the chemical composition is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, maybe we better leave that to someone else. How many instances of such staining did you observe in your tour of the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember at least half a dozen. I remember specific sites. There was on the Stradun. I remember seeing this. I remember seeing -- one of the houses that had been partially burned out. The stop storey and roof were gone, and there was a wall behind the house, and there was this red stain came up along the wall. I remember specifically also in the -- there was an outdoor cinema. In the outdoor cinema we found a tail of 120-millimetre mortar, and on a wall we found also the traces of this kind of stain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Could you give us perhaps more of a general idea as to where this staining was concentrated, if at all?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's really very hard to say. The two examples that I gave you would have been in the -- well, no. In the, they're both south of the Stradun, but one of them is further towards the west wall. And I think the other case is just south of the Stradun, but not very far. Maybe in the middle town area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman, we need to break now because of the tapes. So we will have the second morning break at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is possible. I believe I am very near the end of the examination-in-chief, just so Your Honours are aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you can do it in one minute, you can finish, but otherwise perhaps you might prefer to finish after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before we proceed, I formally wish to tender into evidence two exhibits which currently do not have any means of identification. The first one being the photograph which was tendered showing the staining. I would respectfully request that that be assigned an exhibit number. And furthermore, the map, formerly P13, but pursuant to procedure to date it should be assigned a new exhibit number as well. The map of the old town which Dr. Kaiser drew upon to signify various buildings and edifices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next exhibit number for the photograph will be P64 and the exhibit number for the map will be P65.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, in order to enable us to formally tender your report, which is to be found at tab 5 in the bundle of exhibits which were submitted today, could you tell us when you prepared that report.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The report was prepared in the first couple weeks of the month of January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I see it's jointly authored, you and Mr. Carnez.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You are both familiar, I take it, with the contents of that report?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And the annexes and the photographs appended thereto?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Once again, annex 7 is a table of statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I do apologise to Your Honours. It's not very clear. We will deal with the matter of the quality of the appendices in a few moments. I will address that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: But appendix 7 shows evidence which as you've already mentioned in your evidence was supplied to you by the Institute for Protection of Monuments in Dubrovnik. When was that table actually supplied to you, on what occasion?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was asked to go to accompany a high UNESCO official to the New Year's concert which was organised by minister Kouchner and UNESCO. And so I was in Dubrovnik very briefly on the afternoon/evening of the 31st of December for New Year's.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You went to a concert.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was given to me upon -- at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember who gave it to you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was given to me by members of the institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Perusal of your report, though, the main body of your report, allows us to note that you incorporated this annex 7 into your findings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: When did you leave Dubrovnik, sir, for the first time?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time was the 22nd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, before you move on. Is there any concern about the receipt of that document now, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I abide by the position that I put forward this morning when the testimony of this witness began. As there are substantial amounts of overlap between this report at tab 6 as far as I know and not tab 5, as my colleague has repeatedly said. And the exhibit which has been marked as 51, I believe it would be meaningful to draw a distinction as to who did what and when and who signed what. And then you could have our position. Very frequently during this examination-in-chief, I personally was not clear as to which specific documents were being referred to, specifically as relates to tab 6. Once this distinction is drawn, I believe we shall have further clarification from Mr. Kaiser, and I don't think we shall then be facing any further problems as to the authorship of these respective reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: May I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, this is being tendered now on the basis that it was a report co-authored by Dr. Kaiser. Contains work undertaken by others under his guidance as well as his own, but work which were -- according to a system which he established and the result is one which he has accepted and adopted as his own. In those circumstances, my inclination is to suggest that there is a sufficient adoption and identification and authentication of the document to make it admissible in whole. The weight that might be attached to work done by others if there was a factual dispute about a particular piece of damage and the report of Dr. Kaiser indicates that the assessment of that damage was done by somebody other than himself. That would appear to be a matter of weight to be assessed by the Chamber, rather than admissibility. Now, would you want to put anything further about that view of the matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The Defence shares your view; however, during our cross-examination we will challenge all these issues in view of the fact that even this last document that my colleague has referred to is, as has been said after all, merely an abstract from a different document. Therefore, we are certain to challenge to accuracy of all these conclusions on cross-examination. Your view of that, of course, is final and we have no intention of making further objections to that. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. If it's not contrary to your wish, Mr. Kaufman, with you standing there I'm about to admit the document on the basis indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before you do that, I would just like to clarify, because I understand maybe from Mr. Petrovic's earlier submission that he might be slightly confused as to the documents to which we have been referring to during the evidence today. Just so that Mr. Petrovic's mind is set at rest and I do thank Your Honour for your suggestion as well. We are talking about two reports: The reports which Your Honour is proposing to admit and to which Mr. Petrovic agrees, and I also am grateful for Your Honour admitting it in that manner, is P51 MFI. That's the document which I had attempted to introduce through the witness, Lucianja Peko. There is one further report, and that was the substance of the last question which was put to the witness. That's the report which was co-authored by Dr. Kaiser and Mr. Bruno Carnez and that's to be found in the new bundles that were placed before Your Honours this morning. That is entitled "Rapport sur l'etat du patrimoine culturel". I won't continue in French. But its English translation is: Report on the Status of the Cultural Heritage in the Old Town of Dubrovnik following the Bombardments of October, November, and December, 1991. That is Dr. Kaiser's report as opposed to the institute's -- for the protection of monuments in Dubrovnik reports which is currently marked P51 MFI. So I will now sit down and respectfully request once again that P51 MFI be admitted into evidence as a formal exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And not the report of Dr. Kaiser.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And the report of Dr. Kaiser, of course, but with a separate exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I am too confused to understand what my colleague is saying, but my understanding is: He is bringing up the issue of what is actually inside tab 6. We have spoken about that. That's what I was discussing. This morning I made a request and my understanding was he shared my view, as regards exhibit 51. That was something that was left for later on. And now if I understand Mr. Kaufman correctly, he wants both admitted right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That seems to be the position. I must say, I too was under a false understanding, Mr. Petrovic. I thought Mr. Kaufman was moving for the admission only of the report which is at tab 6. But we both now understand it is that Mr. Kaufman seeks to have admitted that report at tab 6 and also the report of the institute which is at the moment marked for identification as P51. Now, you want to speak about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Of course. What I said applies to the report at tab 6. As for exhibit 51 and the report therein, we spoke about it at length last week, and it was the Chamber's conclusion that the modality of admission of this exhibit into evidence would depend on this witness's testimony, and we did say that again this morning. Suddenly I realise again now that before I even had occasion to question this witness my colleague is trying to push both these exhibits into evidence. Mr. Kaiser's report at tab 6 cannot be challenged at all. However, I fail to see why we must try to now what may or may not be the Chamber's decision following Mr. Kaiser's testimony and after the Defence team has been given an opportunity to question the witness on Exhibit 51, among other things, which now has only been marked for identification even in relation to Exhibit 51, the witness has not even been shown this exhibit. The witness was not made to go through this exhibit, and yet an admission is being requested for this document. Your Honours, may we please leave Exhibit 51 for later following this witness's testimony. As for tab 6, we are fully agreed on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you content, Mr. Kaufman, for the question of the admissibility of P51 MFI to await your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I would submit that I have prepared the ground for the admission of P51 by virtue of the questions that I have asked the witness today. And I am prepared to make legal submissions on that matter; I could do it now, I could do it later. So perhaps in order to avoid -- to save time, I think it's better that we do it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we should move on. And in re-examination if you would move the admission, if the Chamber wants legal submission, it will ask you for it. The report which Dr. Kaiser co-authored which is at tab 6 will now be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps at this point in time I could ask for the full bundle to be received, as it as -- rather, two bundles as it were, formally, because they have only been marked for identification presently, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The bundles that are presently marked for identification as P63, including tab 6, will be received and will become Exhibit 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, to conclude your evidence in-chief, Dr. Kaiser, I would request the assistance of Mr. Usher, and we will place a number of photographs on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Now, these are to be found in the annexes, tab 6, to Dr. Kaiser's report. I do apologise for the quality of the photographs. This is an appropriate opportunity for me to perhaps make a suggestion. The photographs which are going to be presented on the ELMO are better photocopies than the photographs which are contained in Your Honours' bundles. The reason why the photographs are of such a poor quality is that they have been through -- not just this trial, but another trial which is currently being conducted in this institution. So therefore, as in the evidence of a previous witness, we have photocopies of photocopies. But the copies currently in Dr. Kaiser's possession are better photocopy versions. What I would suggest and request is that Dr. Kaiser's photographs be submitted to the Trial Chamber and kept by the Trial Chamber until judgement, whereupon they may be returned to Dr. Kaiser. We -- in the meantime, by we, I mean the Office of the Prosecutor, will endeavour to obtain the colour originals from UNESCO archive headquarters, and hopefully and by the time Mr. Janicot gives evidence in the following weeks we will have the colour photographs which I believe are currently in the archives of UNESCO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, are you happy to relinquish the copies you presently have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not happy to relinquish them, but I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your reluctance is well understood. We thank you. They will be taken into the custody of the Chamber. We're going to see them first, are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: We are indeed, Your Honours. They are premarked so to aid Mr. Usher in his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: The first photograph, if we could perhaps turn to that, Dr. Kaiser, tell us the symbol we see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The symbol you see on this protection work is the symbol of The Hague convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the next photograph. It's photograph number 7. Now, earlier, sir, you took us through a number of projectiles. Perhaps you could tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the variant of the winged projectile which we saw on the drawing. It's clear there's a tail structure. Little wings here and this is the cylinder I mentioned, which doesn't have any ribbing around it. It is smashed at the top, which I believe comes simply because it struck something which was stone. The stone of Dubrovnik is kind of limestone. It's extremely hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we might be able to see a better example of that in the next photograph, number 8, the limestone. Perhaps you could take us through that assortment of items. Tell us where they were, what they are.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here, here, and here you see the same projectile as the one in the preceding photograph. What you see here is, in fact, probably plaster, which means that the projectile has gone into a wall somewhere. And the plaster or pour cement which is what that looks like. This is a mortar tail here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And the fins, can you point that out?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fins of the mortar tail here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the bigger mortar; this is not the small one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Just for the -- sorry, sir. Just for the sake of clarity, from where were these items collected?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I should -- these were items that we found in the institute when we came there on the 27th of November. These had been collected in the town but I'm not 100 per cent certain everything came from within the town. We did have the occasion to see other ordnance which -- we did not see anything in the town that seemed to indicate the damage that had actually been done by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Would these items be characteristic of the types of items that you would have found in the Old Town after the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would be, basically except for these little ones down here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on, shall we. Photograph number 9. You see a hand. What's that hand pointing to or positioned by?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is on the walls of Fort St. John. The hand is there to give the dimension of the crater, and this is a crater we believe caused by one of these winged projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Of what calibre?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: 82-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Next photograph, please, number 12. Just for the sake of example, what would we see here?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a picture taken from the damage of the earlier period and this is damage to a roof on the small port, presumably from one of these -- the winged projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And once again because it's from an earlier instant, would this be characteristic of the type of damage you would have observed after the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was damage -- yes, there was damage like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And the last photograph, please. Yes, a further example.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the Dominican Monastery, and this is damage done on the 6th of December. You can see three shots that are sort of roughly equidistant. And this was done by the-- that winged projectile, the 82-millimetre. I should just say that we called - we called it - "the rocket," and if I use that word you will at least which projectile to which I'm referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Just so it's clear, Dr. Kaiser, on the image presented on the screen in front of us it said paragraph 12 and the rocket impact went to 20 -- 82-millimetre during the bombardments of November. But the photograph below, you said, shows the Dominican Monastery and what the "petit arsenal," which I believe is the small arsenal. So could you perhaps just clarify: The photograph underneath photograph 13 refers to the Dominican monastery?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, it's photograph 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: And the last photograph, please, photograph number 18. What is that item?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the tail end of a Malyutka rocket. And you can see quite clearly that the coiled -- the wire around the mechanism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher, for your assistance in this matter. Perhaps if that bundle could be submitted to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, we will ensure that you get a copy for safe keeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this bundle as well as the photographs will be the appendices as well, because I am aware, of course, that the appendices are not of the best quality. Once again, I do apologise. We will endeavour to produce the best possible copy at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, are you proposing that these have a separate exhibit number or simply be in the custody of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I suggest that they be in the custody of the Trial Chamber, Your Honours, with the caveat that I mentioned earlier that upon receipt of better evidence they be returned to Dr. Kaiser since they are his personal belongings. I would of course request that my learned friend Mr. Petrovic, who has just risen to his feet, have full access to those copies because I am aware that the copies that he has are of the same nature and quality that the Trial Chamber has currently in their possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now they are copies of -- can you give me the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: It would be P63, Your Honour, as admitted today. It's the appendix -- the last appendix to tab number 6. In fact, it's all the appendices plus the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, all I want to ask is: From a practical aspect, how shall we familiarise ourselves with these photographs, the copies that we have here are of poor quality and the ones that Mr. Kaiser has brought are much better. That's one thing I want to know. And since I am on my feet I would also seize this opportunity to ask about the other documents in this report that are not perfectly legible, all the tables and the sketches. I believe that my colleague will include these in his efforts to obtain the originals, because these copies are quite poor and it is very to discern anything in these tables, sketches, and drawings, providing graphic representation of the impacts in the area under discussion. I believe an effort will be made to obtain clearer copies of these, because based on these copies we have now it will prove difficult to ask specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: If I may address that issue, in fact the reason why I ask for all the appendices to be submitted is because the ones in Dr. Kaiser's personal report, copy of the report which has just been submitted to the Trial Chamber are of a very good quality. It's just that the photographs are not of a good quality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With respect to the photograph, Mr. Petrovic, can I suggest you liaise with the Court officer once we have risen, and you will be able, I'm sure, to make arrangements to view the photographs before we continue on Monday. And better quality of the other annexes to Dr. Kaiser's report are going to be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Last questions. You mentioned JNA officials and officers and troops that you might have seen and saw. What about Croatians? Croatian military presence in the Old Town, did you see any?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a few occasions we saw individual soldiers who were in the Old Town. A small number of soldiers is not unusual. I mean, we know that there were soldiers who lived in the city, so -- but there were very, very small numbers of people we saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I've already asked you a question when I was asking questions about the ramparts, whether or not you saw mortars on the ramparts, as was alleged by certain JNA officials in the meetings that you had with them. Did you ever see any military hardware in the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a few long weapons that were carried by soldiers, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, long weapons.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be automatic weapons. I assume these were the weapons the soldiers were carrying with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, you were in Dubrovnik for three months -- sorry, for the month of November and part of the month of December.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: About three weeks finally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Three weeks finally. I do apologise. You witnessed the damage of the 6th of December, 1991. In a few words, how would you encapsulate that damage to a World Heritage Site?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few words. It was really extensive damage for a morning's bombardment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Dr. Kaiser, I thank you very much. If you could wait there, there will be some more questions from Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you sit, Mr. Kaufman, did you mean to tender the two documents that were identified by Dr. Kaiser and developed in his evidence or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: If I could be reminded as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One was the weapons. They're each part of 51, but do you want them separately tendered or just left as part of 51?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I don't think there's any need to burden the Court with extra exhibits in this matter. I am conscious of the fact that I didn't ask for a separate exhibit number to be assigned to these particular items because they are already in fact contained in P51 which is currently marked for identification. Hopefully I will succeed in convincing Your Honours that this exhibit should be tendered in its entirety. Should I not succeed, which I hope not be the case, then I will have to request that Your Honours accept those items in their individual form. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I ask the usher -- we shall probably be fortunate enough to have two lecterns by the end of the trial; that will save some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Kaiser, I am Vladimir Petrovic, an attorney at law. On behalf of the defence of Pavle Strugar, I will put a few questions to you about your testimony, if you agree. I would like to go back briefly to your education, your formal education. Is it correct that you are a historian by formal education?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you have a Ph.D.?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A D.Phil., which is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the topic of your D.Phil. dissertation was?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The title of my dissertation is: The Masters of Request, an Extraordinary Judicial Company in a Period of Centralisation, 1590 to 1660.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, before 1991, did you ever work for UNESCO?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked for the International Council on Monuments and Sites, which is a nongovernmental organisation, which works closely in conjunction with UNESCO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you concluded a contract with UNESCO, were you given any formal training by UNESCO?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how did UNESCO first learn about what was happening in Dubrovnik? I'm referring to October and November 1991. On the basis of what did they get this information?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were receiving faxes directly from Dubrovnik. That I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there any other source of information?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what other sources of information there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Before your arrival in Dubrovnik, did you know what sort of conflict this was and who the warring sides were?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what you knew and how you came by this knowledge.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I do read the newspapers and I do follow the events. I have been given to understand from my reading of the medias that the Former Socialist Republic of Croatia had seceded from the federal republic -- Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what kind of conflict was this, between whom, and what exactly was happening in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict was between the federal forces, that is the army of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Croatian defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you know this when you set out on your mission?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please: Who were the members of your mission in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were in fact two observers, two representatives. The director-general -- I was one of the people, and the other person was Mr. Bruno Carnez, a UNESCO functionary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Mr. Carnez was the chief of your mission?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What were the responsibilities of the chief of the mission and what were your responsibilities as a member of the mission?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the mission was responsible for all the political contacts that would be -- that would take place. I was responsible for my -- for the work of dealing with the damage survey and making the recommendations about restoration of cultural heritage. I was a consultant. That's a different thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Carnez also an expert on evaluating the extent of the damage and the kind of damage?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is he -- was he also an expert, if I understand the question correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't the expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was his profile?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a -- you mean what is his background?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What I mean is: What was his job within UNESCO?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm trying to remember exactly what Mr. Carnez did at that time. He was attached to the bureau of external relations in UNESCO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the UNESCO memorandum about the mission within the framework of the convention on the protection of cultural heritage. Do you know of such a document?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you're referring to the letter which was written to me by the director-general of UNESCO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does this letter define your task?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there a plan to visit other cultural historical monuments that were part of the World Heritage List, apart from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly an attention on the part of UNESCO to visit other sites that were on the world -- that were on the World Heritage List, such as the Plivice lakes. Our mission was targeted on Dubrovnik, but there had been some vague discussion that eventually we would go -- we could go on to see the Plivice lakes, but there was no time, there was no possibility to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any of the faxes arriving in the UNESCO headquarters from Dubrovnik and do you know what their content was?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw some of the faxes before the mission. I wasn't there when the faxes came in. I don't remember them very well, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Why did you go to Belgrade first?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Belgrade -- the Belgrade step of the mission took place with Mr. Janicot, Mr. Vogric, Mr. Carnez, and myself. The objective was to discuss the route that the mission would take in order to go to Dubrovnik. There was a discussion about the -- I think the desire was to confirm the engagements of the federal authorities vis-a-vis the World Heritage Site.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why to Belgrade? Why didn't you do this in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The federal authorities whom we -- these were state-level authorities of the federal republic. It was normal that UNESCO would go to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: UNESCO then applied to their authorities that were their counterparts in negotiations?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know or do you recollect whether at that time the UNESCO representative in Paris was still accredited by the federal state at the time under discussion?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At that time was all the correspondence and cooperation between your organisation and Yugoslavia, did it go through that channel of communication, if you know?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can't really answer that because I was new to UNESCO and I was only a consultant. Those are internal relations in the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you had any talks in Belgrade in the federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs and, if so, how many such meetings there were. And at what level these meetings were held, if you can, were held, if you can recollect that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the building of the ministry of foreign affairs and I can only remember one big meeting. And I remember, because I mentioned that General Pujic was there. I do not remember who the other officials and other officers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were these separate meetings -- were there separate meetings in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the general staff, or was it all one meeting?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And that meeting was attended by representatives of the army as well as the representatives of the government?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was the main item on the agenda at these meetings the protection of the world heritage, that is of the city of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a major part of the discussions, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that all these people were familiar with what was happening in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did appear so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask these questions about the shellings you had probably learned about from the faxes sent by the Croatian side in October and November? Did you ask them what had happened, under what circumstances, how? Did you raise the issue?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a junior member of this mission and as a consultant, I didn't raise any questions at this meeting. The actual discussion about damage, I don't think it was raised by our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When I say "you," I don't mean you personally, but your entire delegation. Tell me: Why was such a disturbing issue not raised on your side?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue of the protection of the town was of course raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask something else. The alleged attack on a world heritage site was a very important issue. How is it possible that it was not raised before higher-ranking civilian and military authorities in Belgrade, and if this was not raised, why wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was explained to the authorities there by Mr. Janicot and what the roles of the people in the mission were, and it was explained that I was going as the expert and I would be looking at war damage and make some proposals for restoration. In other words, the question of damage was diplomatically and indirectly raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But the threat of damage was very serious. Didn't you express your serious concern?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the director of the cabinet of the director-general was there to introduce a mission to go to Dubrovnik, I think the seriousness of the situation was, in fact, fully underlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I won't insist on this. Were you interested in whether there had been any investigation into the event of October and November in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. By "investigation," you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you interested in whether the federal authorities had conducted an investigation into the events of October and November, which was the occasion of your arrival? Did you ask about that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not ask any questions about such an investigation. The subject was not raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did your organisation formally request an investigation - I don't mean your delegation, but the institution to which you belonged?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't properly answer that because I was not privy to correspondence, I was not privy to other contacts that had been made by the organisation with the federal authorities before I arrived on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you were in Paris preparing for your trip, did you receive any briefing?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember one meeting with the director-general, Mr. Janicot, Mr. Vogric, and Mr. Carnez, and it was a meeting to explain to us what we were supposed to do. But I don't remember all of that particular discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you perhaps told what side was causing the damage, if any?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the documents that had come through seemed to be indicating that the side that was causing the damage was the -- were the federal forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The only documents you had at the time were the documents arriving from the Croatian side. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in considering what I was able to see at the time briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you try to remember, please, General Pujic, the person you talked to. Can you remember anything about that person, his rank perhaps, his official position, or anything at all about him, where the meeting took place, anything at all about this meeting.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it took place in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. It didn't take place on the ground floor; it was several floors up. I remember an array of officers from the federal army, a certain number of diplomats. I was not informed -- maybe we were not informed of the names of all the people around the table. I don't retain a very good -- very, very vague sense of the individuals. It was not such a long meeting; we saw them only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did General Pujic tell you about what the task of the JNA was in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general talked -- he talked generally about the situation in Croatia and he referred to the situation as an "armed riot". He gave some indications about foreign mercenaries, Croatian paramilitaries who would be functioning in the Dubrovnik area. He made some indications, I believe, about the number of cease-fires that had taken place and which -- there may have been 13, and 12 of them had not been respected by the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was your view on what he told you at the meeting? Did you believe that, as you had previously believed faxes from the Croatian side? Or did you perhaps have doubts? And if so, why?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you remember perhaps UNESCO is perhaps a little bit circumspect on some things. Certain questions and not asking, because perhaps the only information at the time was written on faxes. After all, the reason I was sent there was to ascertain if there was war damage. Now, later on I believe that you could see easily in the media, there was a certain number of reportage about what was going on in Dubrovnik. But the whole intention of the organisation was to treat the matter in as fair and impartial way as possible. Mr. Janicot did not hurl any accusations across the table at the federal authorities, military or political authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time did you recognise as true the information that mortars were placed along the bottom of the walls, because you were told exactly that by a high state official in Belgrade, or were you inclined to doubt that bit of information also? You did not have your own people on the ground, so all you know is what the two parties are telling you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the whole point, I mean to say that they are -- there's shelling damage in the town and then to say there are mortars at the foot of the walls. I mean all these things are things that have to be demonstrated. You listen to them, you note them down, but you cannot possibly make a judgement upon them because you have not been there to see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you also told in Belgrade how exactly you could travel to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were told. I can't remember the exact itinerary but basically it would have been down the territory, Republic of Serbia, Republic of Montenegro, and across -- we would go across to Cavtat, and then take a federal boat from Cavtat to Dubrovnik. This would have been the itinerary. This was the itinerary that was outlined by the federal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave to the Prosecutor in 2001 to the investigators of this Tribunal. You said that Mr. Janicot had said the following: That you needed a partner to talk to on the JNA side. He received the answer that he should speak to the secretariat and the secretariat should inform those that were in charge of Dubrovnik. Do you remember that specific sentence?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Which secretariat is being referred to here, in as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the secretariat of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who were the people who would then have been in charge of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe's he's talking about those who were in charge of Dubrovnik -- of the Dubrovnik sector, and those would be federal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did they specify who?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- I'm sorry, sir, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Further in your statement, Mr. Janicot pointed out that members of the UNESCO mission should be accommodated in the Old Town, that this had been organised by the mayor of Dubrovnik, and that you would inform the Federal Government as soon as you arrived. Is that an accurate reflection of your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Did you, in fact, ever inform the Federal Government about what was going on in Dubrovnik, first of all the fact that you arrived and also what was going on?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we -- we didn't have a direct means of informing the Federal Government. Our headquarters knew that we had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever try to get in touch with the Federal Government?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself did not try to get in touch with the Federal Government.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did it perhaps under the circumstances strike you as necessary, given what you found upon your arrival in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should point out that Mr. Carnez travelled to Cavtat on one occasion. I do not know who he met in Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did any Federal Government officials, any of those you talked to in Belgrade, perhaps make a request that a federal team should join you in Dubrovnik and carry out an on-site investigation in cooperation with you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discussion -- there was a discussion about the possibility - I think it was suggested by the federal side - of experts being attached to a mission. It was felt that -- on the UNESCO side that the best and the most impartial way to carry out a mission would be only with the UNESCO functionaries. This I think is the logic of the UNESCO position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you turned down this proposal by the federal authorities to have a team sent down there and join you in your investigation on the spot?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This idea was put to one side for the time being by UNESCO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did General Pujic perhaps request on behalf of the JNA for representatives of the federal conservation institute to be sent down to Dubrovnik, along with your team?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure who made the suggestion from the federal side. It could perhaps have been General Pujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you refer to General Pujic requesting that a federal delegation be sent as well as representatives from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs making the same request. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made the statement a few years ago. And I stand by what I made in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I could read exactly what it says here. "The federal Minister of foreign affairs confirmed that we were allowed to carry out our mission and requested that we take steps immediately, saying also that he would like to send JNA experts on the way to provide assistance should any damage be ascertained." Do you still stand by this portion of your statement??

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you saying the federal minister of foreign affairs confirmed. I remember this statement. I'm not -- I stand by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you keep any notes during your stay in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I took specific notes for the damage survey of October and November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What happened to those notes?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I still have those notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hand over a copy of those notes to the OTP when you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was not asked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hand over notes from your meetings in Belgrade to the OTP? Did they perhaps make inquiries about those and perhaps asked you to hand those over to them?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hand over my notes to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
